extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, legal scholars, human rights advocates and policymakers interested in blasphemy laws and freedom of expression
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative, encyclopedic overview of blasphemy, religious insult and related offences across jurisdictions, including national statutes, international human rights guidance, repeal campaigns, and notable cases. Useful for readers seeking legal standards, penalties, and human-rights commentary on laws criminalising insults to religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICCPR limits on freedom of expression (Articles 19 & 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 19 obliges states to guarantee freedom of opinion and expression; paragraph 3 of Article 19 allows certain restrictions on freedom of expression that are 'necessary' and 'provided by law' to safeguard reputations, national security, public order, public health or morals. Article 20 obliges countries to prohibit 'propaganda for war or advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions on expression must meet strict tests of legality, necessity and proportionality under Article 19(3); criminal prohibitions must be compatible with Article 20 where they prohibit incitement to violence/hostility. This provides the international-law framework within which blasphemy/religious-insult laws are to be judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN Human Rights Committee General Comment 34 (Paragraph 48) on blasphemy laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 48 states that 'Prohibitions of displays of lack of respect for a religion or other belief system, including blasphemy laws, are incompatible with the Covenant, except in the specific circumstances envisaged in article 20, paragraph 2.' Such prohibitions must also comply with the strict requirements of article 19, paragraph 3, and other ICCPR articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Comment 34 clarifies that blasphemy laws are generally incompatible with ICCPR guarantees unless they fall within narrowly-defined incitement prohibitions under Article 20(2). Prohibitions must not discriminate between religions or believers/non-believers, nor be used to punish criticism of religious leaders or commentary on doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rabat Plan of Action recommendation on blasphemy laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rabat Plan of Action (2012) concluded that, at the national level, blasphemy laws are counter-productive and may result in de facto censure of inter- and intra-religious dialogue, debate and criticism. It recommended that 'States that have blasphemy laws should repeal these as such laws have a stifling impact on the enjoyment of freedom of religion or belief and healthy dialogue and debate about religion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rabat emphasises repeal as the preferred response, and underscores that the right to freedom of religion or belief does not include a right to be free from criticism or ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN Special Rapporteurs' joint statement on 'defamation of religions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Three UN Special Rapporteurs stated that 'the difficulties in providing an objective definition of the term "defamation of religions" at the international level make the whole concept open to abuse.' They observed that domestic blasphemy laws can be counter-productive, afford different levels of protection to different religions, and have often been applied in a discriminatory manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The joint statement functions as a cautionary standard: because the concept is ambiguous and definitional problems exist, laws framed as protection of religions risk abuse and discriminatory enforcement; states should therefore exercise caution and avoid broad criminalisation of insults to religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Council of Europe Recommendation 1805 (2007)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe adopted Recommendation 1805 (2007) that 'blasphemy should not be a criminal offence' and set guidelines for member states in view of Articles 10 (freedom of expression) and 9 (freedom of thought, conscience and religion) of the European Convention on Human Rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recommendation encourages member states to refrain from criminalising blasphemy and to interpret freedom-of-expression guarantees protectively; it is a regional normative standard advising decriminalisation or non-use of criminal sanctions for blasphemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 295A (India): 'deliberate and malicious intention' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code criminalises 'deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings' by insulting religion or religious beliefs. It was introduced to prevent 'hate speech that insults or attempts to insult the religion or the religious beliefs' of any class of citizen with deliberate and malicious intention to outrage their religious feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike English common law, Section 295A requires proof of the defendant's 'deliberate and malicious intention' as a mental element. Although framed to maintain public order in a multireligious society, Section 295A has been used to restrict free discussion and has led to calls for repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Israel: Insult to religion (Penal Code Article 170)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 170: 'Insult to religion' – If a person destroys, damages, or desecrates a place of worship or any object held sacred by a group, with the intention of reviling their religion, or in the knowledge that they are liable to deem that act an insult to their religion, then the person is liable to three years' imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory provision criminalises physical desecration with an intent/knowledge element. The page notes the law has been rarely enforced, but provides a sentencing example (right‑wing activist sentenced in 1997).

rubrics_metrics.name: Israel: Injury to religious sentiment (Penal Code Article 173)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 173: 'Injury to religious sentiment' – Liability to one year's imprisonment if a person (1) publishes a publication that is liable to crudely offend the religious faith or sentiment of others; or (2) voices in a public place any word or sound that is liable to crudely offend the religious faith or sentiment of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision criminalises certain public speech/publications that are 'liable to crudely offend' religious sentiment; the standard is phrased around the likely offensiveness to others rather than specific intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myanmar Penal Code Chapter XV (Sections 295–298): offences relating to religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XV enumerates offences: 295 Injuring or defiling place of worship with intent to insult a religion; 295A Deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings; 296 Disturbing religious assembly; 297 Trespassing on burial-places; 298 Uttering words, etc., with deliberate intent to wound religious feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 295 and 295A carry a maximum penalty of two years' imprisonment, a fine, or both; sections 296–298 carry up to one year's imprisonment, a fine, or both. The code shares origins with other British-era penal codes; the provisions have been used in prosecutions (examples cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thailand: Sangha Act and penal-code prohibitions on insulting Buddhism
rubrics_metrics.description: Thailand's 1962 Sangha Act outlaws insults or defamation of Buddhism and Buddhist clergy, including damaging statues of the Buddha; stealing, buying or taking them out of Thailand; taking photos of them; sitting with feet facing them; touching them on the head; and wearing tattoos depicting the Buddha. The 1956 penal code (sections 206 and 208) also outlaws insulting or disrupting places and services of any religion recognised by the Thai government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations range from 1 to 7 years imprisonment, and fines of 2,000 to 14,000 baht. Foreign visitors are explicitly warned about these prohibited acts. The listed specific acts illustrate the scope of what can be criminalised under cultural-religious-protection laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nepal: Section 9.156 criminalising 'hurting of religious sentiment'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 9.156 of a new criminal code act (passed 8 August 2017, in force 17 August 2018) serves as a blasphemy law in Nepal, criminalising the 'hurting of religious sentiment' and carrying a penalty of up to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 20,000 Rupees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of recent legislative enactment criminalising religious offence in a country transitioning its penal code; the provision establishes a broad offence of hurting religious sentiment with specified penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of discriminatory application and persecution under blasphemy laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous observations that blasphemy laws 'afford different levels of protection to different religions' and have often been applied in a discriminatory manner, with examples of persecution of religious minorities, dissenters, atheists and non‑theists as a result of such legislation or overzealous application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a substantive evaluative criterion: laws that are vague, discriminatory in application, or offer unequal protection are flagged as problematic and likely to contravene human-rights norms; examples across jurisdictions are cited to illustrate misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaigns and jurisprudential trend toward repeal/decriminalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic global campaign ('End Blasphemy Laws') and legislative reforms in many countries (France, Sweden, Norway, Netherlands, Iceland, Malta, Canada, New Zealand, Greece, Ireland, Scotland, etc.) have resulted in repeal or abolition of blasphemy offences in numerous jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trend and comparative data serve as an implicit standard for assessing domestic laws: the existence of an international movement and regional recommendations (Council of Europe, Venice Commission) supports decriminalisation as a policy benchmark. The page lists jurisdictions and dates as empirical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definitions and mental‑element distinctions (comparative point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative point emphasised: some jurisdictions require a mental element (e.g., 'deliberate and malicious intention' in Section 295A India and equivalent provisions), while others criminalise acts or expressions based on their likely offensiveness regardless of intent (e.g., Israel Article 173's 'liable to crudely offend').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or drafting laws, attention to mens rea (intent) versus objective offensiveness is a key legal-design criterion because intent requirements narrow criminal liability and reduce risk of arbitrary or discriminatory enforcement.
